title: Prompting Claude Opus 5: A Detailed Guide
author: Modelverse Editorial
excerpt: A comprehensive guide on prompting Claude Opus 5, covering behavioral differences, fast mode, and thinking capabilities.
body:
# Claude Opus 5 Just Landed — Here's What Changes at the Prompt Level

Anthropic released its fourth new model in under two months yesterday, and the pitch this time is different. Mythos 5, Fable 5, and Sonnet 5 all arrived as capability stories. Opus 5 arrived as a cost story: Anthropic says it closes in on Fable 5's frontier-level intelligence at roughly half the price, while costing exactly what its predecessor, Opus 4.8, cost. It's now the default model behind Claude Max and the strongest one available to Claude Pro subscribers — which tells you where Anthropic thinks the bulk of everyday work should happen.

That's the press-release version. The part worth your attention, if you're actually building on these models, is quieter: Opus 5 behaves differently enough from 4.8 that prompts tuned for the old model will underperform on the new one. Here's what's actually changed.

## It stopped waiting to be told to double-check itself

The single biggest shift is that Opus 5 verifies and corrects its own work by default. If your system prompt has a line like "double-check your answer before responding" or "use a subagent to verify," that instruction now works against you — it stacks on top of behavior the model already does unprompted, burning tokens for no quality gain. The fix is subtraction, not addition: strip out verification scaffolding you built for older models and let Opus 5's native self-checking do the job.

The flip side is that it narrates more while it works. In agentic sessions, Opus 5 tends to announce what it's about to do and talk through its progress more than 4.8 did. If you're building a user-facing product, that's worth taming explicitly — tell it when to speak up (before the first tool call, when it changes direction, when it's done) rather than leaving the cadence to chance.

## Effort, not thinking mode, is your main lever

Anthropic's framing for Opus 5 leans hard on a single dial: effort. Where thinking mode used to be the main way developers traded cost for depth, effort now does more of that work — low and medium settings hold up well on most tasks at a fraction of the tokens, and you save the highest setting for genuinely hard coding and agentic work. If you were carrying over effort defaults from 4.8, it's worth re-testing them; the sweet spot has moved.

Response length moved too, independently of effort. Opus 5's conversational replies and the documents it writes to disk both run longer by default than 4.8's did. Turning effort down thins out the model's internal reasoning, not necessarily what it says back to you — so if you want shorter answers, you have to ask for that directly rather than assuming a lower effort setting will do it for you.

## It delegates more — which is great until it isn't

Opus 5 hands work off to subagents more readily than previous models, and when a task is genuinely large and parallelizable, that's a real win: fewer agents stepping on each other's output, cleaner writer-verifier splits. The failure mode is the opposite case — small jobs that didn't need delegation getting split up anyway, multiplying cost for no benefit. If your setup supports subagents, it's worth being explicit about when delegation is actually warranted, or capping how many a task can spawn.

## The parts that just got better, no new rules attached

A few upgrades don't come with prompting caveats — they just work:

- **Coding**, especially on multi-file features and larger refactors, where Anthropic says Opus 5 is less likely to leave stubs or placeholders and more likely to finish the whole task if you hand it the full spec up front.
- **Code review**, where it catches real bugs at a high rate without flooding you with false positives, and holds that accuracy even at lower effort — so a fast first pass and a deeper second pass are both realistic.
- **Long context**, with a 1-million-token window Anthropic says stays reliable end to end instead of degrading as you approach the limit.
- **Vision and documents**, particularly charts, UI replication, and multi-sheet spreadsheet work — strong enough that prompt-side workarounds built for older models are worth re-testing, since some may no longer be necessary.

## Why now

The backdrop matters here. Anthropic has shipped four models since June, and enterprise customers have reportedly grown more vocal about unpredictable AI spend over that stretch. Opus 5's whole pitch is turning that unpredictability into something closer to a dial: cheap effort for routine work, maximum effort for output that actually needs it, at a price identical to the model it replaces. Whether that lands depends less on benchmark charts and more on whether the effort parameter delivers a clean cost-to-quality tradeoff on your own workload — the kind of thing you only really learn by running it.

If you're migrating prompts from Opus 4.8, the short version: remove your verification instructions, re-test your effort settings from scratch, and add explicit length and narration guidance if this is going into a user-facing product. Most everything else, Opus 5 handles on its own.

*Reporting based on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 announcement and coverage from Bloomberg, Fortune, CNBC, and 9to5Mac.*
